title: The EU passes the AI Act and its implications for digital medicine are unclear
explain_beginner: When the European Union formally passed its AI Act in March 2024, it became the first broad law anywhere regulating artificial intelligence, and this piece asks a direct question, what does that actually mean for digital health tools and medical AI built or sold in Europe. The honest answer the author gives is that nobody fully knows yet, because much of the law states high level goals and leaves the actual technical detail to standards and guidelines that had not been written when the law passed. A specific unresolved problem is how the new AI law fits together with Europe's existing medical device rules, since digital health tools were already regulated under those rules before the AI Act existed, and it is not yet clear which rules take priority when they overlap. The piece also notes the law does not apply all at once, different obligations phase in over one, two, and three years after passage, which buys time to fill in the missing detail, but does not remove the uncertainty in the meantime.
explain_business: Companies building or selling AI powered digital health tools in the EU should treat this piece as confirmation that the compliance picture was genuinely unsettled at the moment the AI Act passed, not a source of settled guidance, particularly around whether a given product falls under AI Act rules, existing medical device rules, or both at once, since that overlap was not resolved when the law took effect. The staged timeline matters directly for planning, general purpose AI obligations landed first at 12 months, most digital health AI systems at 24 months, and high risk system obligations at 36 months, giving vendors a real but limited window to prepare before enforcement escalates. The practical next step this piece points to, and that had not yet happened when it was written, is the European Commission and AI Office publishing the specific standards and guidance needed to resolve the medical device overlap, so healthcare AI vendors should track that guidance actively rather than assuming current interpretations will hold.
explain_practitioner: Gilbert's commentary examines the EU AI Act as adopted in March 2024 and identifies specific ambiguities in its application to digital health and medical AI, chiefly that the Act's intersection with the existing Medical Device Regulation and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation remains unresolved, creating an open question of which framework governs when a digital health tool is regulated under both. The piece notes the Act's staged implementation timeline, general purpose AI obligations at 12 months, most AI system obligations including many digital health tools at 24 months, and high risk system obligations at 36 months, and observes that regulatory sandbox provisions, despite appearing throughout the text, have no determined operational mechanics yet. As a commentary rather than original research, the piece offers no new data or test, and its stated limitation is essentially the entire argument, the law's practical meaning for medical AI depends on standards, guidelines, and implementing regulations that did not yet exist at the time of writing, so definitive interpretation was not yet possible.
